Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, the authors present resistance CONKAT seq, a clever and significant extension of their
previously published CONKAT seq methodology. By integrating the identification of self-resistance genes, this
new pipeline impressively bridges the gap between biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) discovery and functional
characterization, enabling a targeted approach to uncover natural products with specific modes of action. The
successful identification and validation of the calprotamides as ClpP activators serves as a strong proof of
concept for the power of this approach. Overall, this is a very interesting and well executed study that represents
a notable advance in the field of natural product discovery from metagenomes. The work is certainly worthy of
publication in this journal, pending the satisfactory clarification of the following points.
1, The title is impactful but could be optimized for accuracy. The term "warhead" strongly implies an inhibitory or
destructive mechanism (e.g., covalent inactivation), which is contrary to the reported function of the
calprotamides as activators that enhance ClpP activity. Using a term that more precisely reflects this modulatory
role would prevent potential misinterpretation by readers.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful suggestion. To improve accuracy and avoid
potential misinterpretation, we have replaced the term “warhead” with “motif” in our title and throughout
the manuscript.
2, The rationale for selecting ClpP as the target resistance gene is not clearly explained. A protease is an
unconventional choice for a self-resistance mechanism against a NRPS derived product, making the link non-
obvious to the reader. A brief introduction explaining the hypothesis or prior evidence that motivated this specific
target selection would significantly strengthen the manuscript's logic. This context is crucial for readers to fully
appreciate the discovery pipeline and to adapt this powerful strategy for their own research.
Response:
Selection of ClpP as our target
We developed resistance-CONKAT-seq to identify BGCs encoding natural products that interact with
biologically important protein targets. These targets can include any functionally essential proteins,
whether or not they have known natural product ligands, thereby providing access to new sources of
bioactive molecules with distinct MOAs. We selected clpP for this study because ClpP is a validated yet
underexplored antibiotic target essential for maintaining cellular protein homeostasis, and no ClpP-
targeting compound has reached clinical use. We don’t anticipate any predictable limitations to the
generalizability of the method beyond the need for an essential gene to which you can design degenerate
primers. We believe that resistance-CONKAT-seq can be broadly applied by other researchers to
discover novel BGCs encoding natural products that act on diverse protein targets of interest. To
demonstrate its generality, we have expanded our screening to include two additional target genes, gyrB
and serS, as described in our response to Reviewer 1’s Major Comment 3. We have also clarified the
rationale for selecting clpP in the Introduction.
Conundrum of protease and NRPS-derived product
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful observation. We had not previously considered the possibility
that an NRPS-derived product might be susceptible to degradation by the ClpP system. Fortunately, to
our knowledge, no NRPS-derived natural product is known to be digested by a resistance ClpP protease,
likely due to modifications that limit accessibility to ClpP or the inherent peptide sequence specificity of
the ClpP system. Additionally, the ADEP BGC serves as a relevant precedent, as it contains a clpP
resistance gene and encodes an NPRS product that directly targets ClpP without being cleaved by it.

Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment and the opportunity to clarify this point. We
initially attempted to resolve the full tetradecameric complex using C1 symmetry; however, the resulting
C1 map showed poorly resolved ligand density at all binding sites. This suggested heterogeneity across
the ligand binding sites, potentially due to mixtures of bound/unbound states. To improve the
reconstruction of the ligand, we manually mixed two-protomer units and performed local refinement and
intensive 3D classification. Through this approach, we identified one class of two-protomer units that
showed clear density at the binding site. This focused 3D classification inherently limited the density
quality at the other binding sites. For this reason, we restricted our structural analysis to the two-protomer

to mechanistically explain their different functional outcomes. Because the structure reveals a common

additional information on this topic, please see our discussion of the testable hypothesis suggested by

Response – Comparative analysis of structures and functional outcomes: In our revised manuscript
we now provide a more extensive description of calprotamide A binding to ClpP2 and the comparison of
calprotamide A and ADEP binding (see updated text below). Here we outline what we believe can be
interpreted from our structure as it relates to the activity of calprotamide A in each ClpP activity assay.
Please see the updated text below for how this is now addressed in our revised manuscript.
Peptidase activity: Calprotamide A and ADEP both enhance Mtb ClpP1/P2 peptidase activity. As
calprotamide A and ADEP bind to the same region of ClpP2, this activity enhancement likely occurs
through a shared mechanism. However, previous studies have not resolved the mechanism by which
ADEP enhances peptidase activity, likely due to the limited conformational changes observed in the
Mtb ClpP complex upon ADEP binding. The only notable change that occurs is the formation of an
N-terminal β-hairpin, but no mechanistic hypothesis has linked this structural alteration to increased
peptidase activity. Similarly, in our calprotamide A-bound structure we observed partial ordering of
the ClpP2 N-terminal region and few other conformational changes that might explain the activity
enhancement. The electron density for calprotamide A in our structure indicated only partial ligand
occupancy, which may have limited our ability to capture the full set of conformational rearrangements
induced by ligand binding. Further attempts to prepare cryo-EM grids using higher calprotamide A
concentrations were unsuccessful due to the compound’s low solubility.
Protease activity: Calprotamide A enhances ClpC1-dependent protease activity, whereas ADEP
inhibits this activity by displacing ClpC1 from the ClpP1/P2 complex. Although both ligands bind within
the ClpP2 H pocket, they generate distinct surfaces at the apical region of ClpP2, where ClpC1
interacts. These differing interaction surfaces likely underlie the opposing functional outcomes
observed upon ligand binding. However, without a structure of the full ClpC1–ClpP1/P2 complex, it is
not yet possible to determine how the unique surface formed by the ClpP2–calprotamide A complex
promotes enhanced ClpC1-dependent proteolysis.
Activation of native ClpP: Calprotamide A activates native ClpP, similar to Bz-LL, but this activation
only occurs at elevated ligand concentrations. As noted above, attempts to prepare cryo-EM grids
using higher calprotamide A concentrations were unsuccessful due to the compound’s low solubility.
The testable hypothesis suggested by our structure, which is the main focus of our study:
Our structural analysis of calprotamide A bound to ClpP had the potential to address two different
hypotheses: 1. The mechanistic difference between calprotamide A and ADEP and 2. The existence of
a conserved binding motif between calprotamide A and ADEP. Given the limitations of our structural data,
we were unable to resolve the mechanistic difference between calprotamide A and ADEP and therefore
focused our downstream studies on the second hypothesis. We appreciate the reviewer’s request to
present a deeper mechanistic study, unfortunately this is not possible with our present structure. In place
of this we have expanded our exploration of the second hypothesis and now present an additional study
leveraging the conserved N-acylphenylalanine motif to identify additional ClpP active structures.
Summary of the new N-acylphenylalanine motif study included in our revised manuscript:
In the original manuscript, we focused on identifying N-acylphenylalanine containing molecules from
clpP-associated BGCs. We also presented the observation that a large number BGCs that do not co-
localize with clp genes are also predicted to encode N-acylphenylalanine containing molecules. In the
expanded study we present in our revised manuscript, we synthesized molecules predicted to arise from
a subset of these BGCs. This work identified additional N-acylphenylalanine containing ClpP active
molecules, including two narrow-spectrum antibiotics. One of these compounds inhibits M. tuberculosis
mc2 6206 with a minimum inhibitory concentration of 4 µg/mL.
New text and figures added to the manuscript to address reviewer’s concerns:
Updated text about our structure and calprotamide mechanism (text added for Reviewer 1 in red,
text added in response to Reviewer 2 comment 6 in blue):
“Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure: To explore how the calprotamides affect
ClpP, we determined the cryo-EM structure of calprotamide A bound to Mtb ClpP1/P2. Given the
comparable activity of calprotamide A and B in functional assays, we focused our analysis on
calprotamide A, as calprotamide B is less stable and exhibited low solubility in protein buffer,
making it a poor candidate for preparing high-quality grids. Based on our cryo-EM data, the full
tetradecameric complex could not be resolved under C1 symmetry due to poorly defined density
at the ligand binding sites. We therefore focused on the two-protomer complex and performed
local refinement and intensive 3D classification, which yielded a class of two-protomer units with
improved density at the binding site. All structural analyses reported here are based on the two-
protomer complex.
In our structure, calprotamide A binds the apical surface of ClpP2 at the same general binding
site as ADEP (Fig. 4a-b). The N-acylphenylalanine moiety, shared by both calprotamide A and
ADEP, occupies the ClpP2 H pocket in each structure, and residues forming the H pocket show
no major differences in their interactions with this fragment (Supplementary Fig. 44a). Beyond
this common pharmacophore, the unique structural features of these two natural products largely
extend in opposite directions (Fig. 4c). The electron density for the C-terminal portion of
calprotamide A is less well-defined than that observed for the N-acylphenylalanine motif that binds
the H pocket, suggesting that it is more conformationally flexible. Residues predicted to interact
with the non-N-acylphenylalanine portions of each ligand show only minor side-chain
rearrangements between the two structures (Supplementary Fig. 44b). The largest apparent
difference occurs at R207; however, the electron density for this side chain in the ADEP-bound
structure (PDB 6vgn) is insufficient to confirm a definitive structural change. To further compare
the difference in binding between calprotamide A and ADEP, we performed alanine mutagenesis
of two key residues in Mtb ClpP2, R207 and Q101. R207 forms a salt bridge with calprotamide A
but not with ADEP, whereas Q101 forms a hydrogen bond with ADEP but not with calprotamide
A (Supplementary Fig. 45a). As predicted by our model, the R207A mutation more strongly
impaired calprotamide A-mediated enhancement of Mtb ClpP1P2 peptidase activity than it did
ADEP-mediated enhancement. Conversely, the Q101A mutation had a greater effect on ADEP-
mediated enhancement than on calprotamide A-mediated enhancement (Supplementary Fig.
45b). Whether the unusual bis-γ-lactam bicyclic moiety in calprotamide B forms additional
interactions with Mtb ClpP2 or the ClpP1/P2:C1 complex remains to be determined. It is possible
that the bis-γ-lactam serves primarily to mask the negative charge that would normally be
generated upon release by the thioesterase, thereby improving bioavailability. This is consistent
with the higher cellular accumulation of calprotamide B we observed (Supplementary Fig. 42)
and may help explain its stronger antibacterial activity relative to calprotamide A (Table 1).
Although no major structural rearrangements were observed at the ligand binding site,
calprotamide A binding induced two more distal conformational changes. Specifically, it promoted
ordering of loops in both the ClpP2 N-terminal region and the ClpP2 handle region near the
catalytic sites (Fig. 4d). Notably, changes in these regions have been independently observed in
the ADEP- and Bz-LL-bound structures, respectively. However, while calprotamide A binding
produced electron density consistent with only partial ordering, the corresponding regions in the
ADEP and Bz-LL complexes adopt fully formed secondary structures (a β-hairpin and β-sheet,
respectively). In both the ADEP and Bz-LL structures, all ligand binding sites are fully occupied,
whereas only partial ligand occupancy was observed in our calprotamide A complex. Thus, the
limited conformational changes observed in our structure may reflect an intermediate state
resulting from incomplete ligand occupancy.
Calprotamide A and ADEP both enhance Mtb ClpP1/P2 peptidase activity. As calprotamide A and
ADEP bind to the same region of ClpP2, this activity enhancement likely occurs through a shared
mechanism. However, due to the limited conformational changes observed in Mtb ClpP upon
binding either ligand, the underlying mechanism of activation remains unresolved. Interestingly,
calprotamide A enhances ClpC1-dependent protease activity, whereas ADEP inhibits this activity
by displacing ClpC1 from the ClpP1/P2 complex. Although both ligands bind the ClpP2 H pocket,
they create distinct surfaces at the apical region of ClpP2, where ClpC1 interacts. Based on the
structure of ClpP1/P2 alone, it remains unclear how the unique surface formed by the ClpP2-
calprotamide A complex promotes enhanced ClpC1-dependent proteolysis.” (Line 207-257)

Updated results text (new text in blue)
“The identification of four structurally distinct ClpP active natural products, linked only by their
medium-chain N-acylphenylalanine substructures, suggests that uncharacterized BGCs encoding
this moiety are likely to represent an untapped reservoir of structurally diverse ClpP-targeting
compounds. Notably, this shared substructure that engages the H pocket corresponds to the
smallest ADEP fragment reported to retain antibacterial activity35. Together, our bioinformatic and
activity analyses suggested that the N-acylphenylalanine moiety was likely a previously
unappreciated, yet potentially common, ClpP targeting motif that has convergently evolved in
diverse bacteria. As not all BGCs will contain a self-resistance gene, we carried out a broader
search of sequenced BGCs for those that encode N-acylphenylalanine moieties. This search
identified more than 100 previously uncharacterized BGCs containing an NRPS initiation module
consisting of a phenylalanine-selective A-domain and Cs (condensation starter) domain, which
initiates lipopeptide biosynthesis by appending a fatty acyl chain onto the first amino acid.
Interestingly, a number of the BGCs we identified in both our original clp gene driven bioinformatic
analysis and this broader search are hybrid NRPS-PKS systems indicating that they could encode
both the lipid and the phenylalanine seen in a medium-chain (C6-C8) N-acylphenylalanine motif.
In purely NRPS BGCs, the Cal or Cs initiation domain could instead introduce a primary
metabolism derived medium-chain fatty acid and therefore no specific fatty acid biosynthesis
genes would be required.
While not all these BGCs are expected to encode a ClpP-targeting molecule, this collection is
potentially enriched for ClpP activity. We bioinformatically predicted the encoded peptide
sequences and randomly selected ten uncharacterized BGCs whose products could be predicted
from existing A-domain specificity data, were synthetically accessible, and contained a possible
cyclization site (e.g., serine or threonine) (Supplementary Table 8-9). Most of these BGCs
originated from Actinomycetes species, including four from Mycobacterium, two from
Streptomyces, one from Microbispora, and one from Rhodococcus. The remaining two BGCs
were derived from Paenibacillus and Mucilaginibacter. Each predicted lipopeptide was
synthesized using Fmoc-based solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS) and with the 2-hexenoic
acid lipid moiety from the calprotamides (Supplementary Table 10, Supplementary Fig. 54).
The resulting molecules ranged from five to ten amino acids in length, with ring sizes varying from
four to eight residues. All compounds were evaluated for their ability to modulate Mtb ClpP
peptidase activity and for antibiotic activity against a panel of Streptomyces and Mycobacterium
strains (Fig. 6a). We used an expanded panel of Actinomycetes, as we had previously observed

levels comparable to calprotamide B. Enhancement of ClpP1/P2 activity correlated with
antibacterial activity, with both of these compounds exhibiting antibiotic activity against a narrow
spectrum of Actinomycete species. Notably, myscamide showed potent activity against M.
tuberculosis mc2 6206 with a minimum inhibitory concentration of 4 µg/mL.” (Line 297-333)

Updated abstract text (new text in blue)
“The discovery of natural products with specific modes of action from metagenomes remains
challenging. Here, we present resistance-CONKAT-seq, a pipeline that links biosynthetic gene
clusters (BGCs) to self-resistance genes, enabling identification of metabolites with desired
molecular targets. Using clpP-directed resistance-CONKAT-seq, we identified the calprotamides,
which activate native ClpP and enhance its activity. Cryo-EM and bioinformatic analyses revealed
that the calprotamides’ medium-chain N-acylphenylalanine substructure is a convergently
evolved ClpP-targeting motif and identified additional BGCs predicted to encode this moiety,
including some with co-localized clp genes. The synthesis of structures bioinformatically inspired
by two such clp-linked BGCs, desmethyl jomthonic acid C and tuscamide, revealed that both
enhanced ClpP activity. Extending our bioinformatically guided synthesis study to additional
BGCs lacking nearby clp genes found that ClpP activity enhancement correlated with antibacterial
activity, with the strongest enhancers exhibiting narrow-spectrum antibiotic activity. These
findings establish N-acylphenylalanine as a previously unrecognized but common natural motif
for targeting ClpP, which should help guide the discovery of both natural and synthetic ClpP
modulators for antibiotic and anticancer development. Resistance-CONKAT-seq offers a scalable
method for exploring biosynthetic dark matter for metabolites with desired modes of action.” (Line
21-34)
